caption: Galaxy cluster SpARCS1049+56, imaged by the Hubble and Spitzer space telescopes
story: NASA's two-panel view of SpARCS1049+56 combines Hubble and Spitzer data taken at several wavelengths. At the middle of the picture sits the cluster's largest galaxy, the upper right red dot of a central pair. SpARCS1049+56 is a massive cluster with at least 27 member galaxies and a combined mass of nearly 400 trillion suns, lying 9.8 billion light-years away in Ursa Major.

The giant galaxies at the cores of big clusters usually hold old stars and make new ones slowly. This one is producing about 860 new stars a year, while our Milky Way manages only about one to two. Spitzer's infrared camera picks up the heat of these hot young stars inside dusty regions.

Hubble's visible-light images point to the fuel. A smaller galaxy seems to have merged recently with the central giant and handed over its gas. Hubble spotted "beads on a string", pockets of gas condensing into new stars, which mark a collision between gas-rich galaxies, known as a wet merger.
explore: NASA calls this one of the first known wet mergers at the core of a distant galaxy cluster. The cluster was first found with Spitzer and the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope and confirmed with the W.M. Keck Observatory, both on Mauna Kea. It may be an outlier, or it may reflect an early era when swallowing gas-rich galaxies was common.

understand.summary: A two-panel, multi-wavelength composite pairing visible light from Hubble with infrared light from Spitzer. The colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, so the Spitzer data reveal warm, dusty star-forming regions that no eye could see.

scaleExtra: The cluster lies 9.8 billion light-years away, according to NASA.
alt: A two-panel view of a distant galaxy cluster, with a central pair of objects, the upper right one a red dot marking its largest galaxy.

caption: Galaxy cluster SDSS J1531+3414, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two reddish galaxies sit side by side at the centre, almost encircled by a thin bluish-white ring, with a squiggly blue line just below them. They are a pair of giant elliptical galaxies deep inside SDSS J1531+3414, a dense galaxy cluster in the northern constellation Corona Borealis.

The blue arcs around them are background galaxies whose images the cluster's gravity has bent into streaks. Wound around the two galaxies is something else, a chain of young, blue-white super star clusters 100,000 light-years long, evenly spaced 3,000 light-years apart, twisting like a corkscrew around the cores of the colliding pair. Astronomers first suspected it was another lensed background galaxy, but follow-up work with the Nordic Optical Telescope ruled that out.

The two galaxies are interacting and beginning to share material, and tidal forces from their collision are thought to have shaped the chain. Its even spacing is linked to the Jeans instability, the behaviour of gas clumps held together by their own gravity, much like water from a tap breaking into drops.
explore: Team leader Grant Tremblay of ESO said the structure cannot last long, perhaps about 10 million years, a fraction of the time galaxies take to merge. Its gas may have belonged to the merging pair, cooled out of the hot plasma around them, or been compressed by a shock wave from their crash. The cluster is one of 23 massive lensing clusters in a Hubble programme.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 in visible and infrared light. F390W is shown in blue, F606W in cyan, F814W in yellow and F160W in red.
understand.eye: Part of the data is infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and the colours are assigned to separate filter images rather than recorded as the eye would.

scaleExtra: The corkscrew chain of star clusters is 100,000 light-years long, according to NASA.
alt: Two reddish galaxies at the centre of a field of galaxies, nearly circled by a thin bluish-white ring, with a squiggly blue line below them.

caption: Galaxy cluster Abell 383, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble portrait shows Abell 383, a massive cluster of galaxies. NASA released it with a study of distant supernovae, exploding stars whose light was amplified by the gravity of foreground clusters on its way to us.

A cluster's gravity bends and brightens light from objects far behind it, much as a glass lens bends light, an effect first predicted by Albert Einstein. Astronomers use these natural lenses to find objects too faint to see otherwise. To trust the view they need the lens's "prescription", a map of how strongly it magnifies, and that depends on all of the cluster's matter, including the dark matter that supplies most of its gravity.

Two teams found three supernovae behind different clusters, and two and possibly all three appear to be Type Ia explosions. That type reaches a consistent peak brightness, so comparing the observed and expected brightness measures the magnification directly. Both teams found that the results fit models of the clusters' dark matter.
explore: The supernovae turned up in the CLASH survey, a Hubble census of dark matter in 25 galaxy clusters, and their explosions took place between 7 billion and 9 billion years ago. The astronomers estimate they would need about 20 supernovae spread behind one cluster to map its whole field and confirm a lens model.

understand.summary: Combines visible light from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with infrared light from Wide Field Camera 3. F435W, F475W, F606W and F625W are shown in blue, F775W, F814W and F850W in green, and F105W, F110W, F125W, F140W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: Much of the data is infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the long exposures gather far more light than an eye could.

alt: A Hubble view of the massive galaxy cluster Abell 383.

caption: Protostar IRAS 20324+4057, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Isaac Newton Telescope
story: A knot of gas and dust a light-year long stretches across this view like a caterpillar heading for a meal. The object, IRAS 20324+4057, is a protostar, a star at a very early stage of growth, lying 4,500 light-years away in the constellation Cygnus.

Its shape is imposed from outside. Toward the right edge of the image, 15 light-years from the knot, are 65 O-type stars, among the hottest and brightest known. With 500 fainter but still highly luminous B-type stars they make up the Cygnus OB2 association, thought to hold more than 30,000 times the mass of our Sun. Their winds and ultraviolet radiation are sculpting the knot into its long shape and wearing it away.

That erosion matters for the star inside. Spectra show the central star still drawing heavily on its envelope of gas. Protostars here should grow to about one to ten times the Sun's mass, but if radiation destroys the envelope first, they may end up lighter.
explore: The protostar is still collecting material from the gas envelope around it, and whether it ends up a heavyweight or a lightweight star is not yet settled. The picture blends Hubble data from 2006, taken in green and infrared light, with ground-based hydrogen observations from the Isaac Newton Telescope in 2003, gathered for the IPHAS survey.

understand.summary: A composite of Hubble Advanced Camera for Surveys data and ground-based hydrogen-alpha images from the Isaac Newton Telescope. H-alpha is shown in cyan, F606W in blue and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: The F814W layer records infrared light that the eye cannot see, and the H-alpha filter isolates the glow of hydrogen alone.

alt: A long, caterpillar-shaped knot of gas and dust glowing against a field of stars.

caption: Elliptical galaxy NGC 4150, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Long strands of dark dust stand out against the yellowish core of NGC 4150, an elliptical galaxy 44 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Elliptical galaxies were long thought to have finished making stars billions of years ago, but this one still holds young ones.

Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 found clumps of young, blue stars, significantly less than a billion years old, tracing a ring around the centre that rotates with the galaxy. That stellar nursery is about 1,300 light-years across. From the stars' colours, the team worked out that the burst of star birth began about a billion years ago and has since slowed, while most of the galaxy's stars are around 10 billion years old.

The astronomers believe the fuel arrived with a small, gas-rich galaxy that merged with NGC 4150 around one billion years ago. The young stars contain very few heavy elements, which points to a metal-poor dwarf galaxy about one-twentieth the mass of NGC 4150.
explore: Minor mergers like this are thought to happen up to 10 times more often than clashes between large galaxies, but they leave little trace. Ultraviolet light helps, because it picks out the faint blue glow of hot young stars against the old red stars that dominate ellipticals. Team member Joseph Silk says young stars give at least a third of all elliptical galaxies a blue glow.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, built from several filter images. F814W is shown in red, F555W in green and F438W in blue.
understand.eye: The exposures add up to 3.8 hours, gathering far more light than the eye can, and the colours come from separate filter images.

alt: The yellowish core of an elliptical galaxy crossed by long dark strands of dust.

caption: Virgo cluster galaxy NGC 4660, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble portrait shows NGC 4660, also catalogued as VCC 2000, one of 100 galaxies in the Virgo cluster that Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys examined for globular star clusters. The Virgo cluster, the nearest large galaxy cluster to Earth, contains over 2,000 galaxies and lies about 54 million light-years away.

Globular clusters are dense balls of hundreds of thousands of stars, and they contain some of the oldest stars still shining in the universe. Across the survey, Hubble identified more than 11,000 of them in Virgo, most older than 5 billion years. Its sharp vision separated these fuzzy clusters from stars in our own galaxy and from distant background galaxies, which is hard to do with telescopes on the ground.

The census suggests globulars form more readily where star birth is rapid and intense, rather than evenly from galaxy to galaxy. Dwarf galaxies close to Virgo's crowded centre had surprisingly many globular clusters for their low masses, while dwarfs in the outskirts had fewer.
explore: Many of the globular clusters around M87, the giant elliptical galaxy at the centre of Virgo, may have been taken from smaller galaxies that strayed too close. Astronomer Patrick Cote of the Herzberg Institute of Astrophysics said the results show that how efficiently star clusters form depends on their environment.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. F475W (SDSS g) is shown in blue and F850LP (long pass z) in orange.
understand.eye: F850LP reaches into the near-infrared, beyond what the eye sees well, and the colours come from two separate filter images.

alt: A Hubble view of the galaxy NGC 4660 in the Virgo cluster.

caption: Virgo cluster galaxy NGC 4458, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: NGC 4458, listed as VCC 1146, is one of the galaxies Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys photographed for a census of globular star clusters across 100 members of the Virgo cluster. Virgo, about 54 million light-years away, is the nearest large galaxy cluster to Earth.

Globular clusters are tightly packed swarms of old stars, and studying them helps astronomers understand the early, intense bursts of star formation that built galaxies. Hubble's sharp view let the team identify about 90 percent of the globulars in all its observed fields, which mattered most for small galaxies that have only a handful.

The giant elliptical galaxy M87, at the centre of Virgo, has long been known to host more globular clusters than predicted. Galaxies within 130,000 light-years of it had few or none, which suggests M87 stripped them of their clusters. In M87, globulars poor in heavy elements such as iron outnumber metal-rich ones three to one, and many of the metal-poor ones may have come from dwarf galaxies.
explore: Lead author Eric Peng of Peking University suggests that star formation near Virgo's core was fast and efficient, perhaps driven by dark matter collapsing sooner there, so many globulars near the centre probably formed early in the cluster's history. Farther out, weaker star formation may have produced only less massive clusters that broke apart over time.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. F475W (SDSS g) is shown in blue and F850LP (long pass z) in orange.
understand.eye: The colours are assigned to two separate filter images, one reaching into the near-infrared, so they are not the colours an eye would see.

alt: A Hubble view of the galaxy NGC 4458 in the Virgo cluster.

caption: Open star cluster NGC 6791, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Stars crowd the full field of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, and two background galaxies show through at upper left. This is NGC 6791, an ancient open star cluster 13,300 light-years away in Lyra, whose ordinary stars are estimated to be 8 billion years old. NGC 6791 ranks among the oldest and largest known open clusters, about 10 times larger than most, with roughly 10,000 stars.

Hubble studied the dimmest stars in the cluster, white dwarfs, the burned-out remains of Sun-like stars. Because they cool at a predictable rate, they work as clocks. In NGC 6791 they gave odd readings. One group looked 6 billion years old and another 4 billion, though stars in an open cluster should share one age.

The team found that the younger-looking group may be made of binary pairs, which at this distance blur into single, brighter points that look younger. That leaves two ages to reconcile, 8 billion years for the normal stars and 6 billion for the white dwarfs, which would need some process slowing white-dwarf evolution.
explore: Most star clusters are too far away, and their white dwarfs too faint, for ground-based telescopes to see. Binary stars are common among ordinary stars in NGC 6791 and in many other clusters, but finding them among white dwarfs would be a first.

understand.summary: A composite of exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys in visible and near-infrared light. F606W is shown in cyan and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: The exposures total about 6 hours, revealing white dwarfs far too faint for the eye, and the F814W filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A dense field of stars filling the frame, with two small background galaxies at upper left.

caption: Dwarf irregular galaxy Holmberg IX, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Blue, white and red stars and distant galaxies scatter across a black background, with an irregular, denser grouping of stars at the centre. That loose gathering is Holmberg IX, a dwarf irregular galaxy sitting just off the outer edge of the large spiral M81, 12 million light-years away in Ursa Major.

Hubble resolves more than 20,000 individual stars in the picture. Only about 10 percent are old stars, billions of years in age, while the others are thought to be young, between 10 and 200 million years old. The old and young stars are spread out differently, which may relate to how they formed. Holmberg IX itself is suspected to be a product of an interaction between M81 and its neighbour M82.

Simulations suggest M81, M82 and nearby NGC 3077 passed close to one another 200 to 300 million years ago, and that encounter may have set off the newer star formation. Many small nearby galaxies form stars, but none is as dominated by young stars as Holmberg IX.
explore: Holmberg IX is a Magellanic-type galaxy, similar in size and irregular structure to the Small Magellanic Cloud. Sidney van den Bergh discovered it in 1959 and catalogued it as DDO 66, and it took its present name from Eric Holmberg's study of galaxy groups ten years later. Astronomers hope it will show how such dwarfs act as building blocks of large galaxies.

understand.summary: A composite of two exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. F555W is shown in cyan and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: The F814W filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the colours are assigned to two separate filter images.

alt: A field of blue, white and red stars and galaxies on black, with an irregular, denser grouping of stars at the centre.

caption: Galaxy ESO 325-G004 and the cluster Abell S0740, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The giant elliptical galaxy ESO 325-G004 looms at the centre of a mixed crowd of galaxies. They belong to the cluster Abell S0740, more than 450 million light-years away toward the constellation Centaurus, and ESO 325-G004 alone is as massive as 100 billion suns.

The galaxy's diffuse halo is sprinkled with thousands of faint pinpoints. Each is a globular star cluster, a compact group of hundreds of thousands of stars held together by gravity, orbiting the giant galaxy. Even at this great distance, Hubble resolves them as separate points of light.

Other fuzzy elliptical galaxies are scattered across the frame, and a few have hints of a disc or ring that lends them a bow-tie outline. Several spiral galaxies appear as well. In these, most of the starlight sits in a flat disc and follows the spiral arms, unlike the fuzzy ellipticals.
explore: Science data that Hubble gathered in January 2005 were merged with Hubble Heritage observations made a year later. Filters isolating blue, red and infrared light were used with the Advanced Camera for Surveys to build the three-colour composite.

understand.summary: A composite of many exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. F475W is shown in blue, F625W in green and F814W in red.
understand.eye: The F814W filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the colours are assigned to three separate filter images.

alt: A large, glowing elliptical galaxy at centre surrounded by many smaller elliptical and spiral galaxies.

caption: Spiral galaxy NGC 3370, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The dusty spiral NGC 3370 fills the foreground, its intricate arms spotted with hot areas of new star formation, while far-off galaxies crowd the background. It lies 98 million light-years away in the constellation Leo.

In November 1994 light from an exploding star in NGC 3370 reached Earth. That supernova, SN 1994ae, for a short time outshone every other star in its galaxy, tens of billions of them. It was a type Ia supernova, the kind astronomers use to chart how fast the universe is expanding, and one of the nearest and best observed since modern digital detectors arrived.

Using type Ia supernovae as yardsticks means calibrating their true brightness. Cepheid variable stars, whose regular pulsing reveals their intrinsic brightness, can give the distance to the host galaxy directly. Adam Riess of the Space Telescope Science Institute observed NGC 3370 a dozen times over a month to follow its Cepheids, which only Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys could resolve at the time.
explore: All those visits added up to about one full day of exposure, making this one of Hubble's deepest views and bringing thousands of background galaxies into sight. Riess needed only two filters, covering visual and infrared light, and the Hubble Heritage Project added a blue filter to make the colour picture. His Cepheids here were the most distant yet observed with Hubble.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through visual, infrared and blue filters. The colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: About 25 hours of exposure gathered far more light than an eye ever could, which is why so many faint background galaxies appear.

alt: A dusty spiral galaxy with intricate arms in the foreground, set against a backdrop of many distant galaxies.

caption: Colliding galaxies in NGC 1275, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A dusty spiral galaxy, seen nearly edge-on, appears to spin like a pinwheel while gliding through the larger, bright galaxy NGC 1275. Traces of spiral structure, heavy dust lanes and bright blue patches of active star formation mark the foreground system. NGC 1275 lies about 235 million light-years away in Perseus, at the centre of the large Perseus Cluster of galaxies.

The galaxy behind is a giant elliptical with faint, peculiar spiral structure in its nucleus. They are believed to be crashing together at over 6 million miles per hour. The crash is making gas and dust already in the bright galaxy swirl toward its centre, and X-ray and radio emission from NGC 1275 point to a probable black hole there.

The encounter, which may draw in a few smaller galaxies besides the main pair, is also producing new stars and large star clusters. These clusters resemble the Milky Way's old globular clusters in shape but are far younger, each holding 100,000 to a million stars.
explore: Outside the frame, NGC 1275 shows intricate filaments on a much larger scale, a typical feature of bright galaxies at the centres of clusters. The colour picture combines archived blue and red Hubble data from 1995 by John Trauger and Jon Holtzman with infrared follow-up observations made in 2001 for the Hubble Heritage project.

understand.summary: Built from blue, red and infrared observations with Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2. The colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the exposures total about 4 hours.

alt: A dusty, nearly edge-on spiral galaxy with dark dust lanes and blue patches crossing in front of a large, bright galaxy.

caption: The centre of the Orion Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Glowing gas rises into peaks, valleys and walls across this panorama of the centre of the Orion Nebula, a star-forming region 1,500 light-years away in the sword of Orion. Stitched from a mosaic of 15 fields, it was at the time one of the largest pictures ever assembled from Hubble images.

The view spans 2.5 light-years yet covers only about five percent of the full Moon's area on the sky. Near the centre sit the Trapezium, the nebula's four hottest and most massive stars, whose ultraviolet light heats and lights the gas. Some 700 other young stars are forming here, and jets from some of them drive shock waves that show up as thin curved loops.

The mosaic also revealed at least 153 glowing protoplanetary disks, or proplyds, thought to be embryonic solar systems. Those nearest the Trapezium are losing gas and dust, pushed into tails that point away from the hot stars. Seven more disks appear as dark silhouettes, which let astronomers estimate disk masses of at least 0.1 to 730 times Earth's mass.
explore: The stars here formed from collapsing clouds of gas within the last million years. C. Robert O'Dell of Rice University and Shui Kwan Wong combined 45 separate images to make the mosaic. Images from the European Southern Observatory by Bo Reipurth and John Bally fill out the irregular border at top left.

understand.summary: A mosaic of 45 visible-light images from Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2. Light emitted by oxygen is shown in blue, hydrogen in green and nitrogen in red.
understand.eye: NASA says the overall colour balance is close to what an observer living near the nebula would see.

alt: A wide panorama of glowing, folded gas clouds in the heart of the Orion Nebula, with bright young stars near the centre.

caption: Planetary nebula NGC 2899, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Shaped a little like a moth, or like a single macaroni noodle with its ends turned up, the planetary nebula NGC 2899 stands out against a black sky. Its central band, seen edge-on, is semi-transparent in the middle. Vela, a southern constellation, is its home, approximately 4,500 light-years away.

A planetary nebula is the cast-off gas of a dying star and has nothing to do with planets. NGC 2899 has a cylindrical outflow of gas running diagonally in two directions from its centre. Radiation and stellar winds from a white dwarf of nearly 40,000 degrees Fahrenheit push the gas outward, and a fragmented ring around the middle pinches the nebula like a half-eaten doughnut.

Two companion stars may also be at work near the centre, interacting with each other and helping to sculpt the gas. A forest of gaseous pillars points back toward the star system that drives the radiation and winds. The colours trace glowing hydrogen and oxygen.
explore: NASA released this picture to mark Hubble's 35 years in orbit, as one of an assortment of recent images ranging from Mars to star-forming regions and a neighbouring galaxy. The telescope was carried into low Earth orbit aboard the space shuttle Discovery on April 24, 1990.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. F438W and F502N are shown in blue, F555W and F656N in green, and F814W and F658N in red.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the glow of particular gases, and the F814W filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A moth-shaped planetary nebula with two upturned lobes and a semi-transparent band across its middle, against a black background.

caption: The Little Dumbbell Nebula (M76), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two translucent lobes, mottled with blue, red and orange gas, spread from a thick white band at the centre of the Little Dumbbell Nebula. Catalogued as Messier 76, the nebula lies 3,400 light-years away in Perseus, a northern circumpolar constellation, and Hubble photographed it to mark the 34th anniversary of its launch.

M76 is a planetary nebula, a shell of glowing gas thrown off by a dying red giant star. The white band is a ring of gas and dust seen edge-on, probably shaped by a companion star that the central star may later have swallowed. The star itself is collapsing into a white dwarf, one of the hottest stellar remnants known at 250,000 degrees Fahrenheit, and shows as a pinpoint at the centre.

Two lobes of hot gas escape above and below the ring, driven at two million miles per hour by the outflow from the dying star. Its ultraviolet light makes the gas glow, red from nitrogen and blue from oxygen. The nebula will vanish in about 15,000 years.
explore: Planetary nebulae have nothing to do with planets. Astronomers in the 1700s, using low-power telescopes, thought such objects looked like planets, and the name stuck. A star that appears just below the white dwarf is not part of the nebula and only lies along the same line of sight.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. F475W is shown in cyan, F502N in blue, F656N in green, F658N in red and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: Narrow filters single out the glow of individual gases such as nitrogen and oxygen, and the F814W filter reaches into near-infrared light beyond what the eye sees well.

alt: A nebula of two translucent, multicoloured lobes joined by a thick white band, surrounded by gold-coloured stars.

caption: Globular cluster Terzan 12, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hundreds of thousands of stars crowd together in the compact, beehive-like globular cluster Terzan 12. Stars on the left look redder, while those toward the right are bluish-white. The cluster lies about 15,000 light-years away, in the direction of Sagittarius, deep inside the Milky Way.

That colour shift does not come from the cluster. Gas and dust between us and Terzan 12 absorb and alter its starlight, scattering blue light away and letting mostly redder wavelengths reach Earth. The dust clouds are patchy, so some parts of the cluster look redder than others along our line of sight.

Not every bright star belongs to the cluster either. The brightest red stars are bloated, aging giants many times larger than the Sun, lying between Earth and Terzan 12, and only a few may be members. The very brightest hot, blue stars also lie along the line of sight rather than inside Terzan 12, which contains only aging stars.
explore: Our galaxy's outskirts host about 150 ancient globular clusters, which orbit the galactic centre far above and below the flat plane of the galaxy. Terzan 12 is one of 11 that the Turkish-Armenian astronomer Agop Terzan discovered approximately a half-century ago. Hubble observations have helped show how age relates to composition in the galaxy's innermost globulars.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 in visible and infrared light. F606W is shown in blue, F110W in green and F160W in red.
understand.eye: Two of the three filters record infrared light, which the eye cannot see and which passes through dust more easily than visible light.

alt: A dense, beehive-like cluster of stars, redder on the left and bluish-white on the right, sprinkled with bright stars.

caption: Globular cluster Messier 4, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Thousands of points of light fill a black field, growing somewhat more crowded toward the centre. The most prominent stars look blue or yellow-orange, and the brightest carry four diffraction spikes. This is Messier 4, the closest globular star cluster to Earth, a dense collection of several hundred thousand stars in the constellation Scorpius. NASA has given its distance as both 6,000 and 7,000 light-years.

Astronomers suspect an unseen black hole sits at its core, with a mass of as much as 800 times that of our Sun. That would make it an intermediate-mass black hole, a rare missing link between the small black holes left by exploded stars and the supermassive ones at the centres of galaxies.

Eduardo Vitral of the Space Telescope Science Institute and his team worked out the object's mass from the motions of stars around it, using 12 years of Hubble observations. They found a lot of mass packed into a very tiny region, which Vitral says is hard to explain as anything other than a single black hole.
explore: The alternative would need roughly 40 smaller black holes, by the team's estimate, squeezed into a region just one-tenth of a light-year wide, and such a crowd would be unstable, merging or flinging members out. Vitral cautions that a stellar mechanism unknown to current physics cannot be ruled out. Other suspected intermediate-mass black holes, such as one in Omega Centauri, remain inconclusive.

understand.summary: Taken with the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. F435W is shown in blue, F606W in green and F814W in red.
understand.eye: The F814W filter reaches into near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and the colours are assigned to three separate filter images.

alt: Thousands of blue and yellow-orange stars on a black background, more concentrated toward the centre, the brightest with four diffraction spikes.

caption: Spiral galaxy M100, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two prominent lanes of young, blue stars sweep around the spiral galaxy M100, while its inner region glows yellowish with older populations of stars. Closer in, two tightly wound spiral arms wrap around the core, where a small bar of stars sits. M100 is a grand-design spiral, a name given to galaxies with well-defined, prominent arms.
The arms trace ripples of matter moving through the galaxy's disc of stars. Where they pass, gas piles up into denser regions, and those denser areas trigger new star formation.

Hubble took this picture with Wide Field Camera 3, installed by astronauts on the last space shuttle servicing mission in May 2009, a few months before the photo. M100 holds a special place in Hubble history. In 1993, while NASA prepared to correct a manufacturing flaw in Hubble's main mirror, it was picked as a target to show the planned fix. A blurry picture was taken before the repair, and after the December 1993 servicing mission the galaxy snapped into sharp focus.
explore: NASA released this image to mark the 25th anniversary of the first astronaut servicing mission. M100 was chosen in 1993 partly because it would just fit inside Hubble's field of view. The blurry 1993 view came from the Wide Field and Planetary Camera 1, which astronauts swapped for the vision-corrected Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. The colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The picture combines separate filter images, and NASA does not say how the colours were assigned, so they need not match what an eye would see.

scaleExtra: M100 lies 55 million light-years away, according to NASA.
alt: A spiral galaxy with blue spiral arms around a yellowish inner region.

caption: Spiral galaxy NGC 1309, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble portrait shows NGC 1309, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Eridanus. NASA has given its distance as both 100 million and 110 million light-years. Hubble photographed the galaxy in 2005, 2006 and 2010, years before a weak supernova appeared in it.

That explosion, SN 2012Z, was spotted by the Lick Observatory Supernova Search in January 2012. It belongs to Type Iax, a recently identified class of exploding white dwarfs that are fainter and less energetic than Type Ia supernovae. Curtis McCully of Rutgers sharpened the older Hubble images and found an object at the supernova's position, the first time astronomers had spotted the system behind such a blast.

The team thinks the object is most likely a blue companion star stripped down to its helium core. The white dwarf slowly drew fuel from it until a runaway nuclear reaction set off the explosion, which is thought to leave a battered white dwarf behind, nicknamed a zombie star.
explore: The chance that the object is an unrelated star lined up by coincidence is less than one percent. The team still could not rule out other explanations, including a single massive star that exploded, and planned to look again with Hubble in 2015, once the supernova had faded. More than 30 Type Iax supernovae had been identified by then.

understand.summary: A composite from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. F435W is shown in blue, F555W in green and F814W in red.
understand.eye: The F814W filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and Hubble's sharpness let astronomers pick out a single star system in a galaxy this far away.

alt: A Hubble view of the spiral galaxy NGC 1309.

caption: Starburst galaxy M82 and supernova SN 2014J, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble composite pairs a mosaic of the starburst galaxy M82 with a view of the supernova SN 2014J, which exploded inside it. M82 lies approximately 11.5 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Ursa Major.

A starburst galaxy is one forming new stars far faster than an ordinary galaxy. The mosaic of the galaxy comes from Hubble observations made in March 2006. The supernova view was taken on January 31, 2014, as the explosion approached its peak brightness.

Astronomers using a telescope on the ground discovered SN 2014J on January 21, 2014. NASA describes it as the nearest supernova of its type found in the past few decades. A supernova is the explosion of a star, and for a short time it can rival the light of a whole galaxy.

understand.summary: Built from Hubble Advanced Camera for Surveys observations. F435W is shown in blue, F555W in green, F658N (hydrogen-alpha) in orange and F814W in red.
understand.eye: The galaxy mosaic gathers 13.7 hours of exposure, far more light than an eye collects, and the F814W filter reaches into near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A Hubble composite of the galaxy M82 with the 2014 supernova SN 2014J.

caption: Giant elliptical galaxy A2261-BCG in the cluster Abell 2261, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The giant elliptical galaxy at the centre of this Hubble image outweighs and outshines every other member of the galaxy cluster Abell 2261, three billion light-years away in Hercules. Known as A2261-BCG, it spans a little more than one million light-years, about 10 times the diameter of the Milky Way.

Astronomers expected a concentrated peak of light at its centre, marking a central black hole and the stars around it. Instead, Hubble found starlight spread fairly evenly, filling a diffuse core about 10,000 light-years across. That is the largest core yet seen, and more than three times larger than the centres of other very luminous galaxies.

Two explanations have been proposed. A pair of merging black holes may have stirred up the stars and flung them outward. Or the merged black hole may have been kicked out of the centre altogether, leaving the stars without an anchor so they spread out even more.
explore: In the second scenario, a merger of black holes of unequal mass could radiate gravitational waves more strongly in one direction, giving the combined black hole a kick of millions of miles an hour. At the time of the release the team was observing it again with the Very Large Array, a radio telescope in New Mexico, to pin down the black hole, if it exists. Abell 2261 is part of the CLASH survey of 25 massive galaxy clusters.

understand.summary: Combines visible and infrared images from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. ACS F435W and F475W are shown in blue, F606W, F625W and F775W in green, and ACS F814W and F850LP with WFC3 F105W, F110W, F125W, F140W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: About 13 hours of exposure, much of it in infrared light invisible to the eye, gathers far more light than an eye could.

alt: A large, diffuse elliptical galaxy at the centre of a galaxy cluster.

caption: The inner region of spiral galaxy NGC 2976, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: What look like grains of sand across the inner region of NGC 2976 are single stars, hundreds of thousands of them resolved by Hubble. Dusty filaments run through the disc with no clear spiral pattern, and blue dots mark young blue giant stars in the star-birth regions that remain active.

NGC 2976 is a small spiral at the edge of the M81 galaxy group, about 12 million light-years away in Ursa Major. An interaction with that group of hefty neighbours stripped away some of its gas and funnelled the rest toward the middle, which has kept stars forming there for at least 500 million years. Star formation in the outer regions stopped when their gas ran out.

Now the inner disc is running low too. The star-forming zone has shrunk to a patch about 5,000 light-years wide around the core. By measuring the colour and brightness of individual stars, astronomers worked out when they formed and rebuilt the galaxy's star-making history.
explore: Team leader Benjamin Williams of the University of Washington estimates that star birth will end in another 500 million years. At one stage the gas density in the inner regions was about five times higher than today, according to Julianne Dalcanton, who led the ACS Nearby Galaxy Survey Treasury team. Radio maps of hydrogen from the Very Large Array were combined with the Hubble results.

understand.summary: A composite from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. F475W is shown in blue, F606W in green and F814W in red.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp vision separates hundreds of thousands of individual stars, a kind of observation team leader Benjamin Williams calls unique to Hubble.

alt: The inner region of a galaxy filled with countless tiny stars like grains of sand, crossed by dusty filaments and dotted with blue stars.

caption: Part of the Coma Cluster of galaxies, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A bright spiral galaxy at upper left stands out from its neighbours, brighter and bluer than the galaxies around it, with reddish-brown dusty arms against a whiter disc. Those arms suggest it was disturbed at some point. Everything else in the frame is an elliptical, an S0 galaxy or a background galaxy lying far beyond the Coma Cluster.

The Coma Cluster, also called Abell 1656, is one of the densest known collections of galaxies. It holds thousands of them in a sphere more than 20 million light-years across, over 300 million light-years away. This section lies roughly one-third of the way out from the cluster's centre.

Most galaxies in the central part of Coma are ellipticals, featureless, pale goldish-brown balls of old stars, both dwarf and giant. Spirals, with cold gas still forming new stars, sit farther out. S0 galaxies fall between the two, made of older stars with little recent star formation but with some structure such as a bar or ring.
explore: The cluster takes its name from Coma Berenices and sits near the Milky Way's north pole, away from the dust and gas of our galaxy's plane, so it is easy to see from Earth. The data come from a Hubble survey meant to help compare galaxies in crowded and isolated settings, and nearby galaxies with more distant ones.

understand.summary: A composite of exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys in yellow and near-infrared light. F475W is shown in cyan and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: About 12 hours of exposure gathered far more light than the eye can, and one filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A field of galaxies with a brighter, bluish spiral galaxy at upper left.

caption: Spiral galaxy IC 4040 in the Coma Cluster, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This close-up, cut from a larger Hubble view of the Coma Cluster, shows a spiral galaxy catalogued as IC 4040. NASA's description of the full image singles out a bright spiral at upper left, brighter and bluer than its neighbours, with dusty spiral arms that look reddish brown against a whiter disc.

Those arms suggest that galaxy was disturbed at some point in the past. Bright, bluish-white spirals hold clouds of cold gas that are still forming new stars, and in Coma they are found away from the crowded centre.

The cluster around it, also called Abell 1656, is one of the densest known collections of galaxies, with thousands of members spread through a sphere more than 20 million light-years across. Its central region is dominated by elliptical galaxies, featureless balls of old stars, both dwarf and giant. Between the two types sit S0 galaxies, made of older stars but showing some structure such as a bar or ring.
explore: Lying over 300 million light-years away in Coma Berenices, the cluster sits close to the Milky Way's north pole, where little dust from our own galaxy blocks the view. The larger image covers a section roughly one-third of the way out from the cluster's centre.

understand.summary: Cropped from a Hubble Advanced Camera for Surveys image of the Coma Cluster. The colour mapping for this crop is not published.
understand.eye: The underlying image gathered about 12 hours of exposure, far more light than an eye could collect.

alt: A spiral galaxy in the Coma Cluster, cropped from a larger Hubble image.

caption: The Hourglass Nebula (MyCn18), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: An hourglass of glowing gas, its walls covered in an intricate pattern of arc-like etchings, surrounds a dying star in MyCn18. This young planetary nebula lies about 8,000 light-years away in the constellation Musca. Earlier pictures from the ground showed only a pair of large outer rings around a smaller central one, with none of the fine detail.

One theory says an hourglass forms when a fast stellar wind expands inside a slower cloud that is denser at its equator than at its poles. MyCn18 did not fit that picture neatly. The bright elliptical ring at the centre turned out to be a potato-shaped structure tilted at a very different angle from the hourglass, and the hot star thought to have ejected and lit the nebula sits clearly off centre.
Hubble also found a pair of intersecting rings near the middle that look like the rims of a smaller hourglass. An unseen companion star, and its gravity, may be needed to explain the whole structure.
explore: The etchings on the walls could be leftovers of separate shells the star threw off when it was younger, the result of unstable flows, or the work of a narrow beam of matter hitting the walls. Old Sun-like stars swell into red giants, and once one has shed its outer layers, ultraviolet light from the exposed hot core makes that material glow as a planetary nebula.

understand.summary: Assembled from three images taken with Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2. Light from ionised nitrogen is shown in red, hydrogen in green and doubly ionised oxygen in blue.
understand.eye: Each colour isolates the glow of a single gas, and Hubble's sharpness reveals fine etchings that are usually blurred beyond recognition in pictures taken from the ground.

alt: An hourglass-shaped nebula with patterned walls and a bright elliptical ring near its centre.

caption: The Bat Shadow of the young star HBC 672, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A shape like a pair of wings spreads across a cloud in the Serpens Nebula, a stellar nursery about 1,400 light-years away. It is the shadow of an unseen, planet-forming disk around the young star HBC 672, cast onto a more distant cloud, and astronomers nicknamed it the Bat Shadow.

Klaus Pontoppidan of the Space Telescope Science Institute compares it to a lamp. The star is the bulb, the disk is the shade and the cloud is the wall. The disk is puffed up rather than flat, so light escapes straight up but is blocked along the disk's plane. The shadow spans roughly 200 times the length of our solar system, so big that light takes about 40 to 45 days to travel from the star to its visible edge.

Comparing images from different dates, the team saw the shadow move, as if the wings were flapping. A planet on an orbit tilted to the disk may be warping it into a saddle shape with two peaks and two dips.
explore: The team watched the flapping over 404 days. Such a planet would take no fewer than 180 days to orbit and would orbit at roughly the Earth-Sun distance from HBC 672. A low-mass companion star is another possibility, though the team doubts it. HBC 672 is only one or two million years old, and its disk is too small and distant for even Hubble to see.

understand.summary: Taken with the infrared channel of Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. F125W is shown in cyan and F164N in orange.
understand.eye: Both filters record infrared light, which the eye cannot see, so the colours are assigned rather than seen.

alt: A wing-shaped shadow spreading across a cloud from a young star.

caption: The Hubble eXtreme Deep Field, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: About 5,500 galaxies crowd this tiny patch of sky in the constellation Fornax, a small fraction of the full Moon's width. Spirals shaped like our Milky Way and the Andromeda galaxy sit among large, fuzzy red galaxies that have stopped forming stars, and tiny, faint, more distant galaxies are scattered across the field.

This is the eXtreme Deep Field, or XDF, made by combining 10 years of Hubble photographs of the centre of the earlier Hubble Ultra Deep Field. More than 2,000 images from the Advanced Camera for Surveys and from Wide Field Camera 3, which carries Hubble's sight into the near-infrared, went into it. The faintest galaxies are one ten-billionth as bright as the eye can detect.

The red galaxies are remnants of collisions between galaxies, now in decline. The faint specks were like seedlings for today's big galaxies. Most XDF galaxies are seen while young, small and growing, often through violent mergers, and the light from some has travelled for 13.2 billion years.
explore: Its youngest galaxy dates from just 450 million years after the big bang. In 2012 astronomers expected NASA's planned James Webb Space Telescope to be aimed at the field, since its infrared vision suits light from the distant past that has been stretched to longer wavelengths by the expansion of the universe.

understand.summary: Combines visible light from the Advanced Camera for Surveys with near-infrared light from Wide Field Camera 3. ACS F435W and F606W are shown in blue, F775W, F814W and F850LP in green, and WFC3 F105W, F125W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: Hubble returned to this patch over many visits for a total exposure of 2 million seconds, gathering light from galaxies far too faint for any eye, much of it in infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A black field crowded with thousands of galaxies, from large spirals and fuzzy red galaxies to tiny, faint specks.

caption: Star cluster NGC 3603 and its nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A bright, yellow-white cluster of young stars bursts out like an aerial firework above wisps of glowing purple gas. The cluster, NGC 3603, sits at the heart of a nebula 20,000 light-years away in the constellation Carina, and the clouds of gas and dust around it are raw material for new stars.

The scene is less peaceful than it looks, since violent stellar winds and ultraviolet radiation have blown an enormous cavity in the surrounding gas and dust, which leaves the cluster in plain view. Most of its stars were born at roughly one time, yet they vary in size, mass, temperature and colour. Because a star's mass sets the course of its life, a cluster like this holds stars at many stages.
Among its members are some of the most massive stars known. Such stars burn through their hydrogen quickly and end their lives as supernovae.
explore: Clusters like NGC 3603 offer clues to how massive stars formed in the early, distant universe. Being relatively close, it is also a useful lab for the bursts of star formation set off when galaxies collide.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 in visible and infrared light that traces sulfur, hydrogen and iron. F164N ([Fe II]) is shown in red, F128N (Paschen-beta) in yellow, F673N ([S II]) in green, F656N (H-alpha) in blue and F555W in white.
understand.eye: Part of the light is infrared, invisible to the eye, and narrow filters isolate the glow of individual elements, so the colours do not match what an eye would see.

alt: A bright yellow-white star cluster against dark space above wisps of glowing purple gas.

caption: Ring galaxy AM 0644-741, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble portrait shows AM 0644-741, also known as the Lindsay-Shapley Ring Galaxy. It lies 300 million light-years away in the constellation Volans, and NASA classes it as a ring galaxy.

Ring galaxies are galaxies in which much of the light gathers into a broad loop around the centre rather than into spiral arms. Astronomers generally think such rings form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the disc of a larger one. The collision sends a ripple outward through the disc, like the ring that spreads when a stone drops into a pond. As the ripple travels, it squeezes gas clouds in its path, which can trigger the birth of new stars along the ring.
Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded the galaxy through four filters, from blue light into the near-infrared, on January 16/17, 2004, for a total of 2.8 hours.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. F435W is shown in blue, F555W in green, F625W in pink and F814W in red.
understand.eye: The exposures total 2.8 hours, gathering far more light than an eye could, and the F814W filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A Hubble view of the ring galaxy AM 0644-741.

caption: The Stingray Nebula (Hen-1357), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A bright central star sits in the middle of a green ring of gas, flanked by gas bubbles at lower left and upper right. Its companion star lies diagonally above it, at the 10 o'clock position, joined by a faint green spur of gas pulled toward it by gravity. Curved red lines trace gas heated by a shock where the star's wind hits the bubble walls. This is the Stingray Nebula, which in 1998 was the youngest known planetary nebula.

A planetary nebula forms when an aging, low-mass star swells into a red giant and blows off outer layers, and the remaining core heats the gas until it glows. The Stingray's central star heated up enough to light its nebula only within the 20 years before 1998, a change that came surprisingly fast for a low-mass star.
The wind from the star has blown holes in the ends of the bubbles, which act like nozzles that steer escaping gas into two opposing streams.
explore: The companion matters because astronomers have suggested a second star may be needed to form the ring, bubbles and columns of gas. The bridge of gas toward it was something never seen before in a planetary nebula. At one-tenth the size of a typical planetary nebula, the Stingray is small, so no details were visible before Hubble observed it.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2. F658N (nitrogen) is shown in red, F502N (oxygen) in green and F487N (hydrogen) in blue.
understand.eye: NASA says these are the actual colours emitted by the gases, but from Earth the whole nebula appears only as big as a dime seen from a mile away.

scaleExtra: The nebula is as large as 130 solar systems and lies 18,000 light-years away in the direction of the southern constellation Ara, according to NASA.
alt: A bright star inside a green ring of gas, with bubbles to either side, a companion star at upper left and curved red lines.

caption: Star cluster NGC 346 in the Small Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Thin, pale-blue wisps of cloud fill the background, with denser pink clouds laid over them and large arcs of reddish-brown dust. Bright-blue stars light the nebula from within a young cluster. This is NGC 346, home to more than 2,500 newborn stars, in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a small companion of the Milky Way lying 200,000 light-years away in Tucana.

The cluster's most massive stars, many times heavier than the Sun, shine an intense blue. Their radiation and fierce winds batter the gas they formed from and carve out a bubble within the nebula. That nebula, N66, is the brightest H II region in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a hydrogen cloud lit up by the ultraviolet output of hot, young stars.

Such a region shines only as long as its massive stars live, a few million years, so the glow marks the cluster as young. Using two sets of Hubble observations taken 11 years apart, researchers found the stars spiralling in toward the centre, driven by a stream of gas from outside that feeds star formation there.
explore: The Small Magellanic Cloud holds fewer elements heavier than helium than the Milky Way, which makes its conditions similar to those of the early universe. ESA released this image for Hubble's 35th anniversary. It is the first to combine Hubble observations of NGC 346 at infrared, optical and ultraviolet wavelengths.

understand.summary: Combines Hubble observations in infrared, optical and ultraviolet light. The colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: Infrared and ultraviolet light are both invisible to the eye, so parts of this view record light no observer could see.

alt: A cluster of bright-blue stars inside a nebula of pale-blue wisps and pink clouds, with arcs of reddish-brown dust.

caption: Galaxy triplet Arp 274, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Three galaxies appear to overlap in Arp 274, though they may sit at somewhat different distances. The largest, in the middle, looks like a spiral and may be barred. The spiral on the right is strung with bright blue knots of star formation, as is the small, more compact galaxy at far left. The system lies about 400 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo.

Two of the three are making new stars rapidly, while the spiral shapes of two remain mostly intact. Yellowish older stars fill the central bulge of each galaxy, and a bright cluster of stars marks each nucleus. The arms are traced by younger blue stars, alongside pinkish nebulae lit by new star formation, with interstellar dust silhouetted against the stars.
A pair of stars at far right are much closer, inside our own Milky Way. Hubble photographed Arp 274 after the public picked it in a vote held for the International Year of Astronomy.
explore: Arp 274, also known as NGC 5679, won the Space Telescope Science Institute's You Decide competition with 67,021 of the nearly 140,000 votes cast for six candidate targets. The International Year of Astronomy celebrated 400 years since Galileo first turned a telescope to the sky.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 through blue, visible and infrared filters plus one isolating hydrogen. F673N (redshifted H-alpha) and F814W are shown in red, F606W in green and F450W in blue.
understand.eye: NASA says the colours reflect the natural colours of the different star populations, though the infrared filter records light the eye cannot see.

alt: Three partly overlapping galaxies, a large spiral in the middle, a spiral with blue knots on the right and a compact galaxy at far left.
